s: AI assistant, often called an Agent; as opposed to a chatbot that only replies.
Understands one sentence from you, breaks it into steps, calls tools, and actually gets the job done.

• Large model: understands, thinks, decides the next step
  • Planning: breaks the goal into small steps
  • Toolbox: look up trains, order, pay, etc.
  • Memory: the chat and your habits
  • Loop control: runs step by step, decides when to stop

1. You say: “Book me a high-speed train to Shanghai tomorrow”
  2. The assistant splits it: look up trains → pick one → order → ask you to pay
  3. Calls “look up trains” and gets two: 08:00 and 09:30 example data
  4. Holds a seat, tells you, and pays only after you confirm
A chatbot would only say “you can check on 12306”; an Agent goes and does it.

ProblemEarly chat programs (like ELIZA, 1966) only rewrote your words by rules; later voice assistants (like Siri, 2011) roughly relied on fixed, pre-written intents and failed outside them.
Research · findingAfter ChatGPT appeared in late 2022, large models were already good at understanding and writing, but could only “talk”: no live information, and no acting for you.
DesignResearchers let the model write “call a tool” instructions as well as text: ReAct (Yao et al. 2022) has the model alternate “think a step, do a step”; Toolformer (Schick et al. 2023) taught a model to call APIs itself; in June 2023 OpenAI launched function calling.
Why it worksThe large model understands and decides, tools carry things out for real; together, one sentence becomes a finished job.

KA02.no: Lit = your words go into the large model
s: Prompt: what you say plus the instructions to the model; Context: all the text handed to the model this time.
Lets the large model know exactly what you want and what the situation is.

• System instructions: the assistant’s role and rules, e.g. “ask the user before paying”
  • Your words: this request
  • Background: today’s date, your city
  • History: earlier chat and tool results

1. Your words: “high-speed train to Shanghai tomorrow”
  2. The program adds: today is 28 October, you are in Beijing example data
  3. From this the model works out “tomorrow = 29 October”, departing from Beijing
  4. If information is missing (say, no home city), it asks you
The model only sees the text in its context; what isn’t written there, it doesn’t know.

ProblemTraditional voice assistants first had to file what you said under an “intent”, then fill “slots” (date, place…) one by one; say it differently and they often failed.
Research · findingGPT-3 (Brown et al. 2020) found that if the prompt states the request clearly and gives a few examples, the model does it without retraining (in-context learning); InstructGPT (Ouyang et al. 2022) made models better at following instructions.
DesignInstead of hard-coded intents, put the instructions, your words and the background into one piece of text for the model, and let the model understand and fill in the gaps.
Why it worksThe model has seen all kinds of phrasings in huge amounts of text, so it understands natural language more flexibly than fixed rules; with the background in the context it can work out which day “tomorrow” is.
Task breakdown, also called Planning.
Turns a big goal like “book a ticket” into small steps that can each be carried out.

• Goal: a ticket to Shanghai tomorrow, booked
  • Step list: in order
  • Dependencies: look up trains before ordering
  • Adjusting: if a step fails, change the plan

1. Look up tomorrow’s trains to Shanghai
  2. Pick one by your habits (e.g. morning, second class)
  3. Order and hold a seat
  4. Ask you to confirm before paying
  5. Tell you the result
If the 08:00 train is sold out, go back to step 2 and pick another.

ProblemAsking the model for the answer “in one go” makes it easy to skip steps and get complex tasks wrong.
Research · findingClassic AI studied automatic planning long ago (e.g. STRIPS, 1971); chain of thought (Wei et al. 2022) found that having a large model write out the intermediate steps first clearly raises accuracy on complex problems; least-to-most (Zhou et al. 2022) splits a hard problem into sub-problems and solves them one by one.
DesignHave the large model write a step list first, each step small enough to match one specific tool; finish one step, then look at the next.
Why it worksEach small step is simple, easy to get right and easy to check; if something goes wrong, only that step is redone.
Tool use, also called Function Calling.
Lets the assistant really look up tickets and place orders through program interfaces (APIs), instead of making answers up.

• Tool description: name + purpose + parameters
  • Call instruction: what the model writes: “which tool, with what”
  • Executor: the program that really sends the request
  • Result: written back for the model to read

1. The program first gives the model the tool descriptions, e.g. look_up_trains(from, to, date)
  2. The model writes: {"name":"look_up_trains","to":"Shanghai"}
  3. The program sends that request to the ticket service (example)
  4. It gets back: seats on 08:00 and 09:30 example data, and hands that to the model
The model only writes the instruction; the program does the actual work.

ProblemA large model can only write text: it doesn’t know today’s remaining seats, gets sums and live information wrong easily, and may make things up.
Research · findingReAct (Yao et al. 2022) had the model call Wikipedia search in the middle of its reasoning; Toolformer (Schick et al. 2023) taught a model to insert calculator, search and other API calls into its text; both did better than the model alone.
DesignIn June 2023 OpenAI launched function calling: developers describe tools in a fixed format, the model outputs calls in that format, and the program runs them. Since then most large-model providers have roughly offered something similar.
Why it worksThe format is fixed, so programs can read it reliably; the real data comes from tools, and the model only picks the tool and fills in the parameters.
Safety and permissions; the key practice is called Human-in-the-loop: a person confirms important actions.
Stops the assistant from spending money carelessly, doing something wrong that can’t be undone, or being fooled by bad instructions hidden in a web page.

• Permission levels: look-ups are free to use, paying needs confirmation
  • Confirmation step: ask you before paying or deleting
  • Least privilege: only the tools the task needs
  • Log: every call is recorded

1. Look up trains, hold a seat: done automatically
  2. Pay: pause and show “Confirm payment / Pick another train”
  3. You tap confirm → only then is the “pay” tool called
  4. You tap pick another → back to choosing a train

ProblemThe model sometimes misunderstands or makes things up; text hidden in a web page or file can also pose as instructions to trick it (often called “prompt injection”, widely discussed roughly since 2022).
Research · findingComputer security has long had the principle of “least privilege” (Saltzer and Schroeder 1975): every program gets only the permissions it needs to do its job.
DesignSort tools by risk: read-only ones run straight away; anything that spends money or can’t be undone must be confirmed by a person; each tool exposes only the permissions it needs.
Why it worksEven if the model judges wrongly, the worst case stops at “asking you”, so the damage stays under control.
Agent architecture: large model + planning + memory + tools + loop control.
Shows which parts the assistant is made of and what each one does.

• Large model: the brain: understands and decides
  • Planning: splits steps, puts them in order
  • Memory: short-term = this chat; long-term = your habits
  • Tools: the hands that really do things
  • Loop control: repeats, decides when to stop

1. Memory supplies: “you usually leave from Beijing”
  2. Large model + planning: look up trains first
  3. Tools: two trains found
  4. Loop: not done → go round again, until it asks you to pay
Layer 2 slows this loop down step by step.

ProblemA large model on its own answers once and is done: it doesn’t remember, can’t act, and doesn’t check results.
Research · findingAround 2023 many Agent attempts appeared (e.g. Stanford’s Generative Agents, Park et al. 2023, which gave models memory and reflection); Lilian Weng’s 2023 survey summed them up as large model + planning + memory + tool use.
DesignSplit the abilities into separate parts: the large model only thinks, and the other parts add what it lacks — remembering, doing, repeating.
Why it worksEach part has a clear job and can be improved on its own: swap in a stronger large model or add a new tool, and nothing else has to change.
The Agent loop, also called the perception–action loop; a ReAct-style “think–do–look” loop.
Lets the large model get the job done step by step instead of answering in one go.

• Perception: gathers information
  • Planning: the large model thinks of the next step
  • Call tools: the program carries it out
  • Observation: looks at the result, judges whether it’s done
  • Memory: keeps useful information

1. Round 1: thinks “look up trains first” → two trains found
  2. Round 2: thinks “pick 08:00 and order” → seat held
  3. Round 3: thinks “time to pay, ask the user first” → stops and waits for you
  4. 3 rounds in all example number

ProblemA complex task can’t be thought through in one go, and the intermediate results (are there tickets?) aren’t known in advance.
Research · findingThe classic AI textbook (Russell and Norvig, Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach) defines an Agent as something that perceives its environment through sensors and acts through actuators. ReAct (Yao et al. 2022) found on question answering, fact checking, text games and online shopping that thinking while doing, and thinking again after seeing results, beats only thinking or only doing.
DesignWrite “perceive → think → do → look” as a loop, deciding just one step per round.
Why it worksEvery step is based on the real, latest result, so a wrong turn can be corrected in the next round.
Perception: assembling the information this round needs into the context.
Lets the large model “see” everything it needs to decide.

• Your words: this request
  • Environment: date, location
  • Memory: chat history, your habits
  • Last round’s result: what the tool returned
  • Tool descriptions: which tools are available

1. Takes your words: “high-speed train to Shanghai tomorrow”
  2. Adds: today is 28 October, in Beijing example data
  3. Reads from memory: “likes a window seat”
  4. Joins them in a fixed order into one piece of text → hands it to the large model

ProblemA large model has no eyes or ears of its own, and doesn’t know the time or where you are; anything it isn’t given, it can only guess.
Research · findingDevelopers found in practice that the same model gives very different results depending on whether its context is complete and clear.
DesignUse a dedicated step to pick out and tidy the needed information before handing it to the model, including only what matters for this task.
Why it worksThe more accurately the model “sees”, the more reliable its judgement; with less irrelevant information it is also less easily led astray.
Planning, often written as Thought + Action.
Lets the large model decide exactly what to do next, and say why.

• Thought: why do this
  • Action: the tool name + parameters
  • Format: a fixed format, so the program can read it

1. Thought: “I don’t know which trains there are yet, so look them up first”
  2. Action: look_up_trains(to=Shanghai, date=tomorrow)
  3. This is only a piece of text the model wrote
  4. It goes to the next step, “call tools”, to be carried out

ProblemAsking the model to output actions directly makes it easy to pick the wrong tool or skip steps in complex cases.
Research · findingChain of thought (Wei et al. 2022) found that writing the reasoning before the answer raises accuracy on complex problems; ReAct applied this to actions.
DesignEach round, write the “thought” first, then the “action”; the action uses a fixed format the program can read easily.
Why it worksWriting down the reason is like making the model “think it through first”; the thought also lets people see why it acted, which helps track down mistakes.
Observation; reviewing itself after a mistake is called Reflection.
Looks at the tool result and judges whether the task is done or the plan needs changing.

• Tool result: e.g. a train list, order succeeded/failed
  • Judgement: done? continue? change plan?
  • Reflection note: why it failed, kept for the next round

1. Result: seats on 08:00 and 09:30 example data
  2. Judgement: seats, but not ordered yet → not done, go round again
  3. If ordering fails: write down “08:00 is sold out”
  4. Next round, choose 09:30 instead

ProblemThinking without looking, the model carries on as it imagines and never notices when it’s wrong.
Research · findingReAct (Yao et al. 2022) wrote tool results back to the model as “observations”, which cut down on made-up answers; Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023) had the model write a reflection in words after a failure, store it in memory and consult it on the next try.
DesignAfter every tool call, hand the result back to the large model unchanged and let it judge the next step; failure reasons are written down too.
Why it worksReal results are the best signal for fixing mistakes; with lessons written as text, the model “learns from experience” without retraining.
Short-term memory, i.e. the Context Window: the most text the model can read at once, counted in tokens.
Keeps every step of this conversation so the model knows what has already been done.

• Chat history: what you said, what it said
  • Tool log: every call and its result
  • Length limit: beyond it, nothing more fits

1. Round 1’s ticket results stay in the context
  2. In round 2 the model sees them and knows it should order
  3. If the chat gets too long: drop old content, or squeeze it into a summary first
  4. Important things also go into long-term memory

ProblemA large model doesn’t remember the previous call by itself; the history has to be handed over again every time, and the window has a limited length.
Research · findingEarly models had small windows (GPT-3’s was 2048 tokens), which kept growing; but “Lost in the Middle” (Liu et al. 2023) found models are worse at using information placed in the middle of a long context.
DesignKeep only the most relevant content and squeeze old content into summaries; put key information near the beginning or end.
Why it worksWith little but well-chosen information in the window, the model uses it correctly more easily, and computing costs less.

KB06.no: Lit = memory read back into perception
s: Long-term memory; a common method is Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG).
Keeps your habits and documents across conversations, and when needed finds the few relevant ones for the model.

• Memory store: pieces of text kept in a database
  • Vectors: each memory turned into a list of numbers, searched by meaning
  • Retriever: finds the most relevant few
  • Joining: puts them into the context

1. Saved earlier: “usually leaves from Beijing”, “likes a window seat”
  2. This request is turned into a vector and the store is searched for the closest ones
  3. The 3 most relevant are found example number
  4. They go into the context → “window seat” is used when choosing a seat

ProblemThe context window is limited, so not all history fits; and once the chat is closed, its content is gone.
Research · findingLewis et al. proposed RAG in 2020: first retrieve relevant content from an outside document store, then let the model generate; it did better on knowledge questions, and the documents can be updated at any time.
DesignAgents roughly follow the same idea: keep memories outside, and each round retrieve a few as needed and read them back into the context.
Why it worksThe memory store can be large, but only the most relevant bit is read each time — remembering a lot without overfilling the window.
A Large Language Model (LLM), serving as the “brain” of the Agent.
Reads the context and writes thoughts, actions and replies to you.

• Tokenizing: text cut into small pieces
  • Word vectors: pieces turned into numbers
  • Many Transformer layers: understand the context again and again
  • Output scores: score the next character

1. Reads the text assembled by perception
  2. Computes layer by layer, understanding how “tomorrow”, “Shanghai” and “high-speed train” relate
  3. Scores every candidate character and picks the next one
  4. Appends it and computes again, writing “Action: look_up_trains(…)” one character at a time
Layer 3 zooms in on how it computes inside.

ProblemAn Agent needs a “brain” that understands all kinds of phrasing, can reason, and can write a fixed format; traditional rule-based programs can’t do this.
Research · findingThe Transformer architecture appeared in 2017; GPT-3 (Brown et al. 2020) showed that with a bigger model and more data, many tasks can be done without special training.
DesignUse one general large model as the brain, with prompts, tools and memory fitting it to each task, instead of training a separate model for every job.
Why it worksThe model has learned language and common sense from huge amounts of text; for a new task, just change the prompt and tools.
Stopping conditions, including limits such as a maximum number of rounds.
Decides when to end the loop: the job is done, it needs your confirmation, or something has gone wrong.

• Done: the model outputs a “final reply”
  • Waiting for you: something needs your confirmation
  • Limits: at most so many rounds, at most so much cost
  • Errors: a tool keeps failing

1. Round 3: payment needed → stop and ask you
  2. If no tickets turn up: after a full 10 rounds example number → stop
  3. Tell you why: “No seats tomorrow morning — shall I look at the afternoon?”

ProblemWithout a limit, the loop might keep repeating the same actions, wasting time and money.
Research · findingIn autonomous Agent projects popular in 2023 such as AutoGPT, users roughly often saw them going round in circles while costs piled up.
DesignSet several gates at once: stop when the task is done; stop and ask a person before spending money or anything irreversible; stop and explain when over the round or budget limit.
Why it worksHowever well or badly the model judges, the loop is sure to end; at worst it just stops and asks you.
